paragraphs: “Where ... is Zhutchka?” Ilusha asked, his voice breaking.
“Oh, well, my boy, Zhutchka’s gone. He’s done for!”
Ilusha said nothing, but he fixed his eyes on Kolya again, intently. Alyosha caught Kolya’s eye and made another vigorous sign to him, but Kolya looked away, pretending he hadn’t seen.

“He must have run off and died somewhere. He must have died after a meal like that,” Kolya said without pity, though he seemed a little out of breath. “But I’ve got a dog, Perezvon ... A Slavonic name.... I’ve brought him to show you.”
“I don’t want him!” Ilusha said suddenly.

“No, no, you’ve really got to see him ... it’ll cheer you up. I brought him specially.... He’s the same shaggy kind of dog.... Will you let me call my dog in, madam?” He turned suddenly to Madame Snegiryov, in a strangely excited manner.
“I don’t want him, I don’t want him!” cried Ilusha, with a sad catch in his voice. His eyes had a look of reproach.

“You’d better,” said the captain, getting up from the chest by the wall where he had just sat down, “you’d better ... some other time,” he muttered, but there was no holding Kolya back. He shouted hurriedly to Smurov, “Open the door!” and the moment it was open he blew his whistle. Perezvon came tearing into the room.

“Up, Perezvon, beg! Beg!” shouted Kolya, jumping to his feet, and the dog reared up on its hind legs beside Ilusha’s bed. What came next took everyone by surprise. Ilusha started, lurched hard forward, bent over Perezvon and stared at him, faint with suspense.
“It’s ... Zhutchka!” he cried suddenly, in a voice breaking with joy and pain.
“And who did you think it was?” Krassotkin shouted at the top of his voice, in a ringing, happy tone. He bent down, grabbed the dog and held him up to Ilusha.

“Look, old man, see, he’s blind in one eye and his left ear is torn, exactly the marks you described to me. That’s how I found him, right away. He didn’t belong to anyone!” he explained, turning quickly to the captain, then his wife, then Alyosha, then back to Ilusha. “He lived in the Fedotovs’ back yard. It was his home, but they never fed him. He was a stray that had run away from some village ... I found him.... Now listen, old man, he can’t have swallowed what you gave him. If he had, he’d have died, he’d have had to! So he must have spat it out, since he’s alive. You didn’t see him do it. But the pin pricked his tongue, and that’s why he squealed. He ran off squealing and you thought he’d swallowed it. No wonder he squealed, the skin inside a dog’s mouth is so tender ... tenderer than a man’s, much tenderer!” Kolya cried impetuously, his face glowing and radiant with delight. Ilusha could not speak. White as a sheet, he stared at Kolya with his mouth open and his great eyes almost starting out of his head. Krassotkin had no suspicion of it. If he had known what a disastrous and fatal effect such a moment might have on the sick child’s health, nothing would have made him play such a trick. But Alyosha was perhaps the only person in the room who realized it. As for the captain, he behaved like a small child.
“Zhutchka! It’s Zhutchka!” he cried in a blissful voice. “Ilusha, it’s Zhutchka, your Zhutchka! Mamma, it’s Zhutchka!” He was almost in tears.
“And I never guessed!” cried Smurov, sorry he had missed it. “Bravo, Krassotkin! I told you he’d find the dog, and he has!”
“He has found him!” another boy repeated gleefully.
“Krassotkin’s a star!” cried a third voice.
“He’s a star, he’s a star!” cried the other boys, and they began to clap.

“Wait, wait,” Krassotkin did his best to shout over all of them. “I’ll tell you how it happened, that’s the whole point. I found him, took him home and hid him at once. I kept him locked up there and didn’t show him to anyone until today. Only Smurov has known for the last two weeks, but I told him the dog’s name was Perezvon and he never guessed. Meanwhile I taught the dog all sorts of tricks. You should see everything he can do! I trained him so I could bring you a well-trained dog, in good shape, old man, so I could say to you, ‘See, old man, what a fine dog your Zhutchka is now!’ Haven’t you got a bit of meat? He’ll do a trick for you that’ll make you die laughing. A piece of meat, haven’t you got any?”

The captain ran across the passage to the landlady’s rooms, where their cooking was done. Kolya didn’t want to waste any of the precious time, so in desperate haste he shouted to Perezvon, “Dead!” The dog at once flipped over and lay on his back with all four paws in the air. The boys laughed. Ilusha watched with the same suffering smile, but the one who enjoyed the dog’s performance most was “mamma.” She laughed at him and began snapping her fingers and calling, “Perezvon, Perezvon!”

“Nothing will make him get up, nothing!” Kolya cried triumphantly, proud of his success. “He won’t budge if the whole world shouts at him, but if I call him, he’ll be up in a second. Ici, Perezvon!” The dog leapt up and bounded about, whining with delight. The captain came running back with a piece of cooked beef.

“Is it hot?” Kolya asked quickly, in a businesslike way, taking the meat. “Dogs don’t like hot food. No, it’s fine. Look, everybody, look, Ilusha, look, old man. Why aren’t you looking? I’ve brought him, and he isn’t even looking at him.”

The new trick was to make the dog stand perfectly still with his nose stretched out, and then to lay a tempting bit of meat right on his nose. The poor dog had to stand like that, with the meat on his nose and not moving, for as long as his master pleased, maybe half an hour. But Kolya kept Perezvon like that for only a moment.
“Paid for!” cried Kolya, and in a flash the meat flipped from the dog’s nose into his mouth. The audience, of course, showed delight and amazement.
“Did you really stay away all this time just to train the dog?” exclaimed Alyosha, with a note of reproach he couldn’t hold back.
“Just for that!” answered Kolya, in perfect simplicity. “I wanted to show him off at his best.”
“Perezvon! Perezvon,” Ilusha called suddenly, snapping his thin fingers and beckoning to the dog.

“What is it? Let him jump up on the bed! _Ici_, Perezvon!” Kolya slapped the bed, and Perezvon darted up next to Ilusha. The boy flung both arms around his head, and Perezvon licked his cheek at once. Ilusha snuggled against him, stretched out in the bed and hid his face in the dog’s shaggy coat.
“Dear, dear!” the captain kept saying. Kolya sat down again on the edge of the bed.

“Ilusha, I can show you something else. I’ve brought you a little cannon. You remember I told you about it before, and you said how much you’d like to see it. Well, here it is. I’ve brought it for you.”

And Kolya quickly pulled the little bronze cannon out of his satchel. He was in a hurry because he was so happy himself. At any other time he would have waited for the stir over Perezvon to die down. Now he rushed ahead without any thought for the right moment. “You’re all happy now,” he felt, “so here’s something to make you happier!” He was completely delighted himself.

“I’ve wanted this thing for ages. It’s for you, old man, it’s for you. It belonged to Morozov, he had no use for it, he got it from his brother. I swapped a book from father’s bookcase for it, _A Kinsman of Mahomet or Salutary Folly_, a scandalous book published in Moscow a hundred years ago, before they had any censorship. And Morozov likes that sort of thing. He was grateful to me, too....”

Kolya held up the cannon so everyone could see and admire it. Ilusha sat up and, with his right arm still around the dog, gazed at the toy, enchanted. The excitement grew when Kolya announced that he had gunpowder too, and that they could fire it off at once “if it won’t alarm the ladies.” “Mamma” asked straight away to look at the toy more closely, and she was allowed to. She was delighted with the little bronze cannon on wheels and began rolling it back and forth on her lap. She happily gave permission to fire it, with no idea what she had been asked. Kolya showed the powder and the shot. The captain, being a military man, took charge of loading it and put in a tiny amount of powder. He asked that the shot be kept for another time. They set the cannon on the floor, pointed at an empty part of the room, pushed three grains of powder into the touch-hole and put a match to it. There was a magnificent bang. Mamma was startled but at once laughed with delight. The boys stared in speechless triumph. But the captain, looking at Ilusha, was more enchanted than any of them. Kolya picked up the cannon and presented it to Ilusha at once, along with the powder and the shot.
“I got it for you, for you! I’ve been saving it for you for ages,” he said again, in his delight.

“Oh, give it to me! No, give me the cannon!” mamma began begging like a little child. Her face showed a pitiful fear that she wouldn’t get it. Kolya was thrown off balance. The captain fidgeted uneasily.

“Mamma, mamma,” he ran over to her, “the cannon’s yours, of course, but let Ilusha have it, since it’s a present to him. It’s just as good as yours, though. Ilusha will always let you play with it. It’ll belong to both of you, both of you.”
“No, I don’t want it to belong to both of us. I want it to be all mine, not Ilusha’s,” mamma insisted, on the verge of tears.

“Take it, mother, here, keep it!” Ilusha cried. “Krassotkin, may I give it to my mother?” He turned to Krassotkin with a pleading face, as if afraid Kolya would be hurt by his giving the present to someone else.
“Of course you may,” Krassotkin agreed warmly. He took the cannon from Ilusha and handed it to mamma himself, with a polite bow. She was so touched that she cried.
“Ilusha, darling, he’s the one who loves his mamma!” she said tenderly, and at once started wheeling the cannon back and forth on her lap again.
“Mamma, let me kiss your hand.” The captain darted over to her at once and did so.
“And I’ve never seen such a charming fellow as this nice boy,” said the grateful lady, pointing at Krassotkin.

“And I’ll bring you as much powder as you like, Ilusha. We make our own powder now. Borovikov found out how it’s done—twenty-four parts saltpeter, ten parts sulphur and six parts birchwood charcoal. You pound it all together, mix it to a paste with water and rub it through a fine cloth sieve—that’s the way.”
“Smurov told me about your powder, only father says it’s not real gunpowder,” said Ilusha.
“Not real?” Kolya flushed. “It burns. I don’t know, of course.”
“No, I didn’t mean that,” the captain put in, looking guilty. “I only said real powder isn’t made like that, but it doesn’t matter, it can be made that way.”

“I wouldn’t know, you know best. We lit some in a pomatum jar. It burned splendidly and was gone, with only a tiny bit of ash left. But that was only the paste, and if you rub it through ... but of course you know best, I don’t know.... And Bulkin’s father thrashed him over our powder, did you hear?” he said, turning to Ilusha.
“Yes,” answered Ilusha. He listened to Kolya with huge interest and enjoyment.

“We’d made a whole bottle of it and he kept it under his bed. His father found it. He said it might explode, and thrashed him on the spot. He was going to complain about me to the masters. He’s not allowed to go around with me now. Nobody is allowed to go around with me now. Smurov isn’t either. I’ve got a bad name with everyone. They say I’m a ‘desperate character,’” Kolya smiled scornfully. “It all started with that business on the railway.”

“Ah, we’ve heard about that exploit of yours, too,” cried the captain. “How could you lie still on the track? Is it possible you weren’t the least bit afraid, lying there under the train? Weren’t you frightened?”
The captain flattered Kolya abjectly, with no dignity at all.
